title: Cloudflare Workers Review: Pros, Cons, Limits (2026)
summary: Cloudflare Workers review covering capabilities and constraints.
body_markdown:
## Where Activepieces Fits Next to a Worker


If you want to move webhook data between business apps without code to maintain, an Activepieces flow with a webhook trigger does it, and the app on the other end is usually already an integration: the community integrations directory of the open source monorepo holds 747, about 60% contributed by the community, under an MIT-licensed core.


Access control, audit logs and release management come with the same product, whether you self-host it or use the cloud, so the glue around your Workers can be reviewed and traced like the rest of your stack.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production. If a job needs custom logic at the edge, that belongs in a Worker, which the flow can call over HTTP.


### Creating workflows with triggers and steps


Think of Activepieces as a workflow automation tool: you build a flow out of a trigger and a chain of steps, and each step talks to an app you already use.


Give the flow a webhook trigger and it gets its own URL. Whatever system posts to that URL starts a run, so a form submission, a payment event or a support-ticket update can fan out to other tools without anyone writing a handler.


For plain "when this happens there, do that here" plumbing, you skip the deploy, the secrets handling and the retry code that a Worker would make you own.


### Where a Worker takes over


That convenience stops where your logic gets unusual. Signature checks on an odd header scheme, rewriting a payload before anyone sees it, or deciding in milliseconds which region a request should go to are code problems.


For those, a Worker is the right home, and it sits well beside a flow rather than inside it.


The flow makes an HTTP request to the Worker, the Worker does its narrow piece of work and returns a response, and the flow carries on with the result.


A separate Worker sits to the side with an HTTP arrow going out from the flow and a response coming back.


Read it as a division of labor. The flow owns the sequence and the app connections, and the Worker owns only the one step that needs real code.


What the diagram doesn't show is Activepieces replacing Workers hosting. It doesn't run your edge code near users, and it's not a place to put a long-running or stateful job. It's a way to avoid writing glue.


That split keeps your own code small. You maintain a few short, request-shaped functions, which is what Workers handles well, and leave the app-to-app wiring to a tool built for it.
